anchor.text: Bon + jour links good + day. Reuse jour in bonjour and trois jours; greet the shopkeeper before asking for anything.

hello.soundFi: French j is voiced sh, not Finnish j; ou is close to Finnish u. The n in bon marks a nasal vowel.

anchor.text: Picture the server handing you a café: merci pour le café. Attach merci to the moment of receiving something.

thanks.soundFi: The final i is clear, like Finnish i. The r is heard; c before i sounds like s.

anchor.text: Store the whole polite ending after your order: un café, s’il vous plaît. Finnish often puts kiitos in the same position.

please.soundFi: Ou in vous is close to Finnish u. The final s of vous and t of plaît are silent in this phrase.

anchor.text: English pardon has the same spelling. Use Pardon, où est… ? when you need to interrupt someone for directions.

excuse.soundFi: On is a nasal vowel here: do not finish with a separate Finnish n. The final written n marks that sound.

anchor.text: At reception, nod and say oui before j’ai une réservation. Pair the sound with your nod.

yes.soundFi: Oui begins with a quick /w/ glide into i; it is one syllable, not two Finnish vowels said separately.

anchor.text: Practise non, merci as one polite refusal. It is the French partner of Finnish ei kiitos.

no.soundFi: On is nasal in non. Keep the first n, but do not add a separate final n.

anchor.text: Spot jour, day, inside aujourd’hui. Connect today’s date on your phone with this whole word.

today.soundFi: Au sounds like o; ou is close to Finnish u. In hui, move quickly from a y-like French u into i.

anchor.text: Picture moving your train ticket one day forward on a calendar: je pars demain.

tomorrow.soundFi: Ain is one nasal vowel, not Finnish ai + n. Start with a light de, then let the last vowel resonate through the nose.

anchor.text: At the till, point to this moment: je voudrais payer maintenant. Connect the word to pressing Pay now.

now.soundFi: Ain and an mark nasal vowels in this word. Do not read their written n letters as separate Finnish n sounds.

anchor.text: Tap the precise spot on your map and say ici. Pair the short word with your finger on the spot.

here.soundFi: Both i sounds are clear, close to Finnish i. C before i sounds like s.

anchor.text: Learn ici / là-bas as a pointing pair: tap here, then point over there. The gesture supplies the contrast.

there.soundFi: The s at the end of bas is silent. À and a are a-like vowels; the accent does not mean a long Finnish vowel.

anchor.text: Link ouvert with ouverture, opening. Picture pushing the café door and reading ouvert on its sign.

open.soundFi: Ou is close to Finnish u. The final t is silent in ouvert; it is heard in the feminine ouverte.

anchor.text: Imagine a firm shut door and the sign fermé. Practise the sign pair ouvert / fermé.

closed.soundFi: É is an e-like vowel, not a Finnish long ee. The final written é is pronounced; the r before m is also heard.

anchor.text: Nom resembles English name. On a French form, connect NOM with surname and PRÉNOM with first name.

name.soundFi: Om is nasal here: no separate final m. Le nom has two spoken syllables, not a long Finnish consonant.

article.note: Nom is masculine: un nom. Prénom is also masculine. Learn the article with the word, not from Finnish nimi.

anchor.text: Link the verb aider with the noun aide: m’aider asks for help; votre aide thanks someone for it.

help.soundFi: The infinitive ending -er sounds like é, an e-like vowel. Ai at the start is one vowel, not Finnish ai.

anchor.text: Picture Gare d’Angers on the station frontage, then ask Où est la gare ? Connect gare with the building you need.

station.soundFi: G before a is a hard g, not French j. The final e is silent; pronounce the r before it.

article.note: Gare is feminine: une gare. German der Bahnhof is masculine, so its gender does not transfer.

anchor.text: English train is spelled the same way. Keep the familiar meaning while learning its different French sound.

train.soundFi: Ain is a nasal vowel, not Finnish ai + n. Keep the initial tr together and avoid a separate final n.

article.note: Train is masculine: un train. The vehicle itself does not explain the gender; store the two words together.

anchor.text: Tram is familiar from English and German Tram. Picture Angers’ tram and practise je prends le tram.

tram.soundFi: The m is pronounced: this word does not end in a nasal vowel. The single a is not a Finnish long aa.

article.note: Tram is masculine, like tramway, its full form: un tram / un tramway.

anchor.text: Picture your phone displaying a travel billet, then say un billet pour Angers. The destination completes the memory.

ticket.soundFi: Here ill gives a Finnish-j-like glide. The final t is silent; do not pronounce a Finnish double l.

article.note: Billet is masculine: un billet. The same ticket could be feminine la carte in another expression; gender follows the noun.

anchor.text: Imagine looking up at the numbered quai on a departure board, then following it to the platform edge.

platform.soundFi: Qu sounds like k. Ai is one e-like vowel here, not Finnish ai; no consonant follows it in speech.

article.note: Quai is masculine: un quai. Learn this as a fixed pair rather than guessing from the object.

anchor.text: Compare English departure with départ. On a station board, départ is your outgoing journey.

departure.soundFi: The final t is silent; the final r is heard. É is an e-like vowel and does not indicate Finnish vowel length.

article.note: Départ is masculine, while arrivée is feminine. Keep the station-board pair le départ / l’arrivée.

anchor.text: English arrival points toward arrivée. Pair the board headings départ / arrivée: leaving / arriving.

arrival.soundFi: Ée is pronounced as one e-like vowel. The doubled r is not a Finnish long rr.

article.note: Arrivée is feminine; l’ hides la before the vowel. Compare une arrivée with un départ.

anchor.text: English reservation is a close visual anchor. Finish J’ai une… with réservation at a hotel or restaurant.

reservation.soundFi: The ending -tion sounds /sjɔ̃/, not Finnish -tio. Its final vowel is nasal; do not add n.

article.note: Réservation is feminine. Many nouns ending in -tion are feminine; use this as a tendency, not an absolute rule.

anchor.text: Hotelli, hotel, hôtel: the familiar building keeps the same core meaning. Store un hôtel because l’ hides the gender.

hotel.soundFi: The h is silent. Ô is o-like, while the final l is pronounced; do not read an extra Finnish h.

article.note: Hôtel is masculine: un hôtel. The h is silent, so le becomes l’; l’ alone does not tell you the gender.

anchor.text: Picture opening your hotel room with its key: la clé de ma chambre. Keep the room and its key together in memory.

bedroom.soundFi: Ch sounds like sh. Am is nasal before b here; do not insert a separate m between that vowel and b.

article.note: Chambre is feminine: une chambre. The gender is part of the noun, not a property of the room.

anchor.text: Imagine the receptionist placing one key in your palm: voici la clé. Repeat clé while making the turning gesture.

key.soundFi: É is one clear e-like vowel. The k and l stay together; do not add a vowel between them.

article.note: Clé is feminine: une clé. The spelling ending -é does not make it masculine.

anchor.text: English address points to adresse. Picture copying the hotel’s adresse into a map app.

address.soundFi: The double ss gives s, not a Finnish long ss. The last e is silent; the r is still pronounced.

article.note: Adresse is feminine: une adresse. L’ hides la before a vowel; un/une shows the gender clearly.

anchor.text: On your map, draw a left arrow as you say à gauche. Practise it opposite à droite, not as an isolated word.

left.soundFi: Au sounds like o; ch sounds like sh. The last e is silent.

anchor.text: Compare à droite with tout droit. Droite has a heard t and means right; droit in tout droit means straight.

right.soundFi: Oi is a /wa/ sequence, not Finnish oi. The t in droite is heard; the last e is silent.

anchor.text: Draw a straight arrow: tout droit. Contrast it with the turning arrow for à droite; the tiny written e changes the phrase.

straight.soundFi: Ou is close to Finnish u. The final t of droit is silent here, unlike the t in droite.

anchor.text: Revoir connects to seeing again: au revoir is a leave-taking chunk. Say it as you step out of a shop.

goodbye.soundFi: Au sounds like o; oi in revoir is /wa/, not Finnish oi. The final r is pronounced.

anchor.text: Bon + soir means good + evening. Reuse soir in ce soir, this evening, and bonsoir, the greeting.

good-evening.soundFi: On in bon is nasal. Oi in soir is a /wa/ sequence; do not use the Finnish oi diphthong.

anchor.text: Picture waving to a colleague you will meet again shortly: à bientôt. Link it to the next meeting, not a final farewell.

see-you-soon.soundFi: Ien gives a glide into a nasal vowel. Ô sounds like o; the final t is silent.

anchor.text: Accord resembles English accord and Finnish akordi. Picture two people agreeing on the same plan: d’accord.

okay.soundFi: Cc here gives k, not a Finnish long kk. The final d is silent, while the r is heard.

anchor.text: Keep Je ne comprends pas as a ready-made rescue phrase. Connect comprendre with the heard form comprends.

understand.soundFi: Om and en are nasal vowels here. Do not add separate m or n sounds; the final dre keeps its consonants together.

anchor.text: Use the reusable frame parler + language: parler français, parler anglais. The language name is your replaceable slot.

speak.soundFi: The infinitive -er ends in an e-like vowel; its final r is silent. The r in par- is still heard.

anchor.text: English repeat is a useful visual neighbour of répéter. Picture pressing Replay to hear the phrase again.

repeat-verb.soundFi: Each é is a clear e-like vowel. The infinitive -er also ends in that vowel, without a final r sound.

anchor.text: The ending -ment often makes adverbs, like Finnish -sti. Link lentement with lent, slow, and say plus lentement.

slowly.soundFi: En in lent- and -ment is nasal. Keep the t in the middle; do not pronounce the final t of -ment.

anchor.text: Picture a platform clock and hold up your palm: je peux attendre ici ? Pair attendre with the train you are waiting for.

wait.soundFi: The doubled t is not a Finnish long tt. En is nasal, while the final dre is a consonant group.

anchor.text: Imagine selecting a ticket before paying: je voudrais acheter un billet. Attach acheter to the act of choosing the purchase.

buy.soundFi: Ch sounds like sh. The middle e can disappear in normal speech; -er ends in an e-like vowel, not r.

anchor.text: English price is a useful neighbour of prix. Picture the price tag beside the object: quel est le prix ?

price.soundFi: The final x is silent on its own. I is a clear Finnish-i-like vowel; keep pr together.

article.note: Prix is masculine: un prix. Its final x is part of the word even in the singular.

anchor.text: Compare Finnish makasiini as a memory hook, but keep meanings apart: un magasin is a shop where you buy things.

shop.soundFi: The g is hard. The single s between vowels is a voiced z. The final in is a nasal vowel, without a separate Finnish n.

article.note: Magasin is masculine: un magasin. Its gender belongs to the French noun, not to Finnish kauppa.

anchor.text: Finnish farmasia points to pharmacie. Picture the pharmacy’s green cross while asking où est la pharmacie ?

pharmacy.soundFi: Ph sounds like f; c before i sounds like s. The final ie is one i-like vowel, not Finnish ie.

article.note: Pharmacie is feminine: une pharmacie. Many nouns ending in -ie are feminine, but there are exceptions.

anchor.text: Link médecin with English medical and medicine. Picture the medical doctor you need, rather than an academic title.

doctor.soundFi: C before i sounds like s. The final in is a nasal vowel, not Finnish i followed by n.

article.note: This entry uses le médecin. Une médecin is also used for a female doctor; both articles can occur with this spelling.

anchor.text: Compare English hospital with hôpital. Picture the emergency entrance and ask où est l’hôpital ?

hospital.soundFi: The h is silent. Ô is o-like; the final l is heard, so do not drop the whole last syllable.

article.note: Hôpital is masculine: un hôpital. Its silent h lets le shorten to l’.

anchor.text: Toilettes resembles Finnish toaletti and English toilet. Look for the plural sign les toilettes, even for one bathroom.

toilets.soundFi: Oi gives /wa/, not Finnish oi. The double tt is not a Finnish long tt; final es is silent.

article.note: Toilettes is normally feminine plural: les toilettes. Use Où sont les toilettes ?, even for one bathroom.

anchor.text: Aide is the noun partner of aider, to help. In merci pour votre aide, put the whole help event after merci.

help-noun.soundFi: Ai is an e-like vowel here. The d is heard; the final e is silent.

article.note: Aide meaning help or assistance is feminine: une aide. Aide referring to a person can have a different use.

anchor.text: English urgent points to urgence. Picture showing the urgent situation and saying c’est une urgence.

emergency.soundFi: U is close to Finnish y, not Finnish u. G before e is voiced sh; en marks a nasal vowel.

article.note: Urgence is feminine: une urgence. Many nouns ending in -ence are feminine; l’ hides la here.

anchor.text: Téléphone resembles Finnish telefoni and English telephone. Picture the phone you are holding, not an abstract spelling.

phone.soundFi: Both é letters are e-like vowels. The final n is pronounced: -phone does not have a nasal vowel.

article.note: Téléphone is masculine: un téléphone. A phone’s gender comes from the noun, not its user or function.

anchor.text: English battery points to batterie. Attach the word to your phone’s empty battery icon.

battery.soundFi: The doubled tt is not Finnish long tt. The ending -ie is one i-like vowel, not a Finnish ie diphthong.

article.note: Batterie is feminine: une batterie. Learn it beside masculine un téléphone as a paired phone scene.

anchor.text: Link chargeur with charger, to charge. The -eur ending often names a person or device that does an action.

charger.soundFi: Ch is sh; g before e is its voiced partner. -Eur has an open ö-like vowel followed by r.

article.note: Chargeur is masculine: un chargeur. The -eur ending often names a device or a person doing an action.

anchor.text: The familiar Wi-Fi sign is already a memory anchor. Add the French article: le Wi-Fi.

wifi.soundFi: French usually says Wi-Fi with i-like vowels, rather than the English ai sounds. W here is a /w/ glide, not Finnish v.

article.note: Wi-Fi is masculine in this use: le Wi-Fi. Store the familiar loanword with its French article.

anchor.text: Heure is the word repeated in neuf heures and dix heures. Connect it to reading the hour on a clock.

clock-time.soundFi: H is silent; eu is an open ö-like vowel. The r is heard; do not read eu as Finnish e + u.

article.note: Heure is feminine: une heure. The silent h causes l’, which hides the feminine article la.

anchor.text: Picture a morning train and say ce matin, this morning. Pair matin / soir with morning and evening light.

morning.soundFi: The final in is a nasal vowel. There is no separate Finnish n at the end.

article.note: Matin is masculine: un matin. Pair le matin and le soir as two masculine parts of the day.

anchor.text: Après means after and midi means noon: après-midi gives afternoon. Picture the clock moving past twelve.

afternoon.soundFi: Après ends without an s sound. Midi has two i-like vowels; say the two word parts together smoothly.

article.note: Après-midi can be masculine or feminine. Un après-midi is common; une après-midi is also standard.

anchor.text: Reuse the soir from bonsoir: ce soir means this evening. Picture the same street after dark.

evening.soundFi: Oi is /wa/, not Finnish oi. The final r is pronounced.

article.note: Soir is masculine: un soir. Reuse it in le soir, ce soir and bonsoir.

anchor.text: Move your calendar marker one day back and say hier. Pair it with aujourd’hui and demain on a three-day strip.

yesterday.soundFi: The h is silent. I glides like Finnish j into an e-like vowel; the final r is heard.

anchor.text: Circle all seven days of your Angers trip: une semaine. Let one full calendar row anchor the word.

week.soundFi: Ai is an e-like vowel. The n is pronounced here, unlike the nasal ain in train; the final e is silent.

article.note: Semaine is feminine: une semaine. Contrast a full week with masculine un jour, one day.

anchor.text: The jour inside bonjour also counts days: un jour, trois jours. Reuse a word part you have already met.

day.soundFi: J is voiced sh, not Finnish j. Ou is close to Finnish u; the final r is pronounced.

article.note: Jour is masculine: un jour. The related feminine journée often describes a day’s duration or experience.

anchor.text: Picture raindrops on your hotel window and say la pluie. Link pluie with the weather phrase il pleut.

rain.soundFi: Start u from a Finnish-y-like position and glide quickly into i. Do not turn ui into a long Finnish u + i sequence.

article.note: Pluie is feminine: la pluie. Weather words do not share one gender: compare le soleil.

anchor.text: Picture the sun over the Loire and say du soleil. Pair la pluie / le soleil as two weather scenes.

sun.soundFi: The ending -eil is an e-like vowel followed by a Finnish-j-like glide. The last written l is not a separate l sound.

article.note: Soleil is masculine: le soleil, unlike German die Sonne. Learn the French article separately.

anchor.text: Keep il fait chaud for weather and j’ai chaud for feeling hot. Picture the heat reaching you from the sun.

hot.soundFi: Ch sounds like sh; au is o-like. The final d is silent.

anchor.text: Learn the weather pair il fait chaud / il fait froid. The sentence frame stays fixed while the feeling changes.

cold.soundFi: Oi is /wa/, not Finnish oi. The final d is silent; keep fr together without an added vowel.

anchor.text: Count one object with its article: un billet, une clé. French changes un to une with a feminine noun.

one.soundFi: Un is a nasal vowel, not Finnish u + n. Compare une, whose u is Finnish-y-like and whose n is pronounced.

anchor.text: Picture two café cups and hold up two fingers: deux cafés. Attach the number to a tiny order.

two.soundFi: Eu is close to a rounded Finnish ö. The final x is silent alone; it can link as z before a vowel.

anchor.text: Picture three marked days on your travel calendar: trois jours. Say the number with its counted object.

three.soundFi: Oi is /wa/, not Finnish oi. The final s is silent on its own.

anchor.text: Picture four chairs around a restaurant table: une table pour quatre. Let the chair count anchor the sound.

four.soundFi: Qu gives k. Keep the final tr together; the last e is normally silent.

anchor.text: Picture five minutes left on a departure countdown: dans cinq minutes. Count down on one hand.

five.soundFi: In is nasal. On its own, cinq ends with a k sound; do not pronounce the written q as a separate letter name.

anchor.text: Picture the clock at six before a meeting: à six heures. Learn the number inside that clock-time chunk.

six.soundFi: Alone, x sounds like s. Before heures it links as z; before a consonant the final sound can disappear.

anchor.text: Mark seven nights on the hotel calendar and say sept nuits. The written p is your reminder not to sound every letter.

seven.soundFi: The p is silent, but the final t is pronounced. E is an open e-like vowel, not a long Finnish ee.

anchor.text: Picture an eight on the platform clock and say huit heures. Use the clock face as a stable image.

eight.soundFi: Start from a Finnish-y-like position, then glide into i. The final t is pronounced when huit is said alone.

anchor.text: Picture the start time of the first conference session: neuf heures. Store the number with that appointment.

nine.soundFi: Eu is an open ö-like vowel. Neuf ends in f alone, but it becomes v in the common phrase neuf heures.

anchor.text: Picture a ten-euro note when saying dix euros. Attach the number to an amount you can see.

ten.soundFi: Alone, x sounds like s; in dix euros it links as z. Before a consonant the final sound can disappear.

anchor.text: Picture a twenty-euro note and say vingt euros. The note anchors the value while the phrase teaches linking.

twenty.soundFi: In is nasal and g is silent. The t is heard in vingt euros; do not pronounce every written consonant in vingt alone.

anchor.text: Use the fixed frame combien coûte… ? and insert the ticket or coffee. The price tag supplies the meaning.

how-much.soundFi: Om and ien are nasal vowel groups. I in -bien glides toward the final vowel; do not add a final n.

anchor.text: Finnish bussi and English bus give you the meaning. Keep the French sound distinct from English bus.

bus.soundFi: U is close to Finnish y, not Finnish u. The final s is pronounced in bus.

article.note: Bus is masculine: un bus. Its final s is present even when there is only one bus.

anchor.text: Connect arrêt, a stop, with arrêter, to stop. Picture the arrêt de tram sign beside the track.

transport-stop.soundFi: The double rr is not a Finnish long rr. Ê is e-like; the final t is silent.

article.note: Arrêt is masculine: un arrêt. L’ is simply le shortened before a vowel.

anchor.text: Aéro- connects to English aero and Finnish aero-; port resembles airport. Picture the airport departure hall.

airport.soundFi: A and é start two separate vowel sounds here. The final t is silent; the r before it is heard.

article.note: Aéroport is masculine: un aéroport. L’ hides le before the initial vowel.

anchor.text: Taxi and Finnish taksi are almost a ready-made pair. Picture the lit TAXI sign outside the station.

taxi.soundFi: X sounds like ks, as in Finnish taksi. The last i is i-like, not the English ai vowel.

article.note: Taxi is masculine: un taxi. The familiar spelling does not supply its French article.

anchor.text: Picture the car waiting outside your hotel: la voiture. Put the word beside the car keys in your memory scene.

car.soundFi: Oi is /wa/. U is close to Finnish y; the final e is silent, while the r is pronounced.

article.note: Voiture is feminine: une voiture. German das Auto does not predict this noun’s gender.

anchor.text: Vélo is the everyday short form of vélocipède. Picture a bicycle-hire stand when saying louer un vélo.

bicycle.soundFi: É is e-like and o stays a rounded o-like vowel. Avoid the English-style diphthong at the end.

article.note: Vélo is masculine: un vélo. Bicyclette is feminine, so two names for the same thing can have different genders.

anchor.text: Pied means foot; à pied means on foot. Picture your feet tracing the short route from hotel to café.

on-foot.soundFi: Ie glides like Finnish j into an e-like vowel. The final d is silent.

anchor.text: English plan is a useful neighbour of plan. In plan de la ville, picture the city map you unfold to find your hotel.

street-map.soundFi: An is nasal here: do not finish with a separate Finnish n. Keep pl together at the start.

article.note: Plan is masculine: un plan. Carte is feminine, even though both can refer to a kind of map.

anchor.text: Picture the French street sign above the hotel door: rue du Musée. Attach rue to the street, not the building.

street.soundFi: U is close to Finnish y, not Finnish u. The final e is silent; rue is one syllable.

article.note: Rue is feminine: une rue. Learn une rue as the unit rather than trying to derive gender from katu.

anchor.text: English place supplies a visual neighbour. In la place, picture the open town square with café tables around it.

town-square.soundFi: C before e gives s. The final e is silent; the word ends with an s sound.

article.note: Place is feminine: une place. Keep the article when its meaning changes from square to seat or space.

anchor.text: Centre + ville joins centre + town. The compound tells you where the tram is going.

city-centre.soundFi: En in centre is nasal. The double ll in ville is not a Finnish long ll; the last e is silent.

article.note: Centre-ville is masculine because the main noun centre is masculine: un centre-ville.

anchor.text: Picture walking over a bridge across the river: traverser le pont. Link the bridge with the crossing action.

bridge.soundFi: On is nasal and the final t is silent. Do not finish with a Finnish n or t.

article.note: Pont is masculine: un pont. Connect the article to the word; the bridge itself offers no gender rule.

anchor.text: English river is a useful visual neighbour of rivière. Picture the water flowing beside your walking route.

river.soundFi: I before è makes a Finnish-j-like glide. The final e is silent, but the final r is pronounced.

article.note: Rivière is feminine, while fleuve is masculine. The two French river nouns each keep their own gender.

anchor.text: English entry points to entrée. Picture the door with the ENTRÉE sign and an arrow going in.

entrance.soundFi: En is nasal. Ée finishes with one e-like vowel; the last written e does not add another syllable.

article.note: Entrée is feminine: une entrée. L’ hides la; learn it in the pair l’entrée / la sortie.

anchor.text: Connect sortie with sortir, to go out. Picture the SORTIE sign with an arrow leading out of the building.

exit.soundFi: The t is pronounced, while the final e is silent. Ie here ends in a single i-like vowel.

article.note: Sortie is feminine: une sortie. The ending -ie often belongs to feminine nouns, with exceptions.

anchor.text: Près de la gare maps naturally to aseman lähellä. Store the whole landmark phrase, not a one-case translation of de.

near.soundFi: The s in près is silent. È is an open e-like vowel; de is light and often ö-like.

anchor.text: Learn près de / loin de as a distance pair on your map: nearby hotel versus distant airport.

far-from.soundFi: Oin is a glide into a nasal vowel, /wɛ̃/. Do not read it as Finnish oi followed by n.

anchor.text: Face resembles English face: picture two shop fronts facing each other across a street. En face de means opposite.

opposite.soundFi: En is nasal, while face ends with s. The final e of face is silent.

anchor.text: Côté means side: à côté de places something at the side of something else. Picture two neighbouring doors.

next-to.soundFi: Ô is an o-like vowel and é is e-like. The final é is pronounced; an accent does not mark Finnish vowel length.

anchor.text: Place your hotel behind a museum on a tiny map, then point and say derrière le musée.

behind.soundFi: The double rr is not a Finnish long rr. I glides into è, and the final r is pronounced.

anchor.text: Picture a taxi parked directly in front of the hotel door: devant l’hôtel. Keep the taxi and façade in one scene.

in-front-of.soundFi: An is nasal. The final t is silent; do not add a separate n to the ending.

anchor.text: English traverse is a useful neighbour of traverser. Draw your path across the road: traverser la rue.

cross.soundFi: The -er ending is an e-like vowel. S after r stays s here, unlike a single s between two vowels.

anchor.text: English turn is a useful neighbour of tourner. Turn your hand as you say tournez à droite.

turn.soundFi: Ou is close to Finnish u. Infinitive -er ends in an e-like vowel without a final r sound.

anchor.text: Store aller à + destination as a travel frame. Je vais à la gare means menen asemalle; the verb form changes.

go.soundFi: The double ll is not a Finnish long ll. The final -er is an e-like vowel, without r.

anchor.text: Pair aller / venir with go / come. Point away for aller and toward yourself for venir.

come.soundFi: The final r is pronounced in -ir, unlike infinitive -er. Keep the first e light; i is close to Finnish i.

anchor.text: English return points toward retour. Link aller-retour with a ticket that takes you there and back.

return-trip.soundFi: Ou is close to Finnish u. The final r is pronounced, and the last syllable rhymes with jour.

article.note: Retour is masculine: un retour. Pair it with un aller for the outward journey.

anchor.text: Aller means to go and simple means single: un aller simple is a ticket going just one way. Contrast aller-retour.

one-way.soundFi: In simple, im is nasal before p. Keep the p and l, but do not add a separate m after the vowel.

article.note: Aller simple is masculine: un aller simple. The infinitive aller is used as a noun for the outward journey.

anchor.text: Picture the departure board adding ten minutes: dix minutes de retard. Attach retard to the growing delay number.

delay.soundFi: The final d is silent, but the r is pronounced. Re- at the start is light, not a long Finnish ree.

article.note: Retard is masculine: un retard. Keep it in the phrase dix minutes de retard, with de rather than an article.

anchor.text: English correspondence is a visual neighbour, but here correspondance means the train or bus connection you must catch.

connection.soundFi: On and an are nasal vowels. Final ce gives s; do not pronounce a final e syllable.

article.note: Correspondance is feminine. The ending -ance is often a useful feminine clue, with exceptions.

anchor.text: Terminal and terminus point to an endpoint. Picture everyone getting off at the last stop on the line.

final-stop.soundFi: U is close to Finnish y, not Finnish u. The final s is pronounced in terminus.

article.note: Terminus is masculine: un terminus. The final s is part of the singular word.

anchor.text: English conductor is a useful visual neighbour, but conducteur here is the driver. Picture the person driving your tram.

driver.soundFi: On is nasal, u is Finnish-y-like, and -eur has an open ö-like vowel followed by r.

article.note: Conducteur is the masculine form: un conducteur. The feminine form is une conductrice.

anchor.text: English passenger and German Passagier are close visual anchors for passager. Picture the person waiting beside you.

passenger.soundFi: The double ss gives s. G before e gives voiced sh; the final -er ends in an e-like vowel.

article.note: Passager is the masculine form: un passager. The feminine form is une passagère.

anchor.text: Picture one wheeled suitcase rolling from the tram to your hotel. Say ma valise as you take its handle.

suitcase.soundFi: The s between vowels is voiced z, not s. The final e is silent.

article.note: Valise is feminine: une valise. Store the pair with a picture of your suitcase.

anchor.text: English baggage points toward bagage. Count one item on the scale: un bagage, deux bagages.

luggage-item.soundFi: The first g, before a, is hard g; the second, before e, is voiced sh. The final e is silent.

article.note: Bagage is masculine. Many -age nouns are masculine, but la page and l’image show that this is a tendency.

anchor.text: English passport and French passeport share a clear visual outline. Picture handing your passport to reception.

passport.soundFi: The double ss gives s, not Finnish long ss. The final t is silent, while the r is pronounced.

article.note: Passeport is masculine: un passeport. Keep the article even though Finnish passi has no gender.

anchor.text: English reception points directly to réception. Picture the hotel’s front desk, key rack and receptionist.

hotel-reception.soundFi: The ending -tion sounds /sjɔ̃/, not Finnish -tio. Its vowel is nasal; the p earlier in the word is pronounced.

article.note: Réception is feminine. The -tion ending is usually a good feminine clue, not a universal rule.

anchor.text: Picture the lift display climbing from ground level to 1: le premier étage. Remember that the ground floor has its own name.

floor.soundFi: É is e-like. G before e gives voiced sh; the final e does not make an extra syllable.

article.note: Étage is masculine: un étage. Many -age nouns are masculine, with exceptions such as la page.

anchor.text: English ascend, go up, is a visual anchor for ascenseur. Picture the lift arrow moving upward.

lift.soundFi: En is nasal and c before e sounds s. -Eur has an open ö-like vowel followed by a pronounced r.

article.note: Ascenseur is masculine: un ascenseur. L’ hides le; -eur often appears in names of devices.

anchor.text: Picture the staircase curving up from the hotel lobby. Trace it upward while saying l’escalier.

stairs.soundFi: The ending -ier sounds like a Finnish-j-like glide plus an e-like vowel; the final r is silent.

article.note: Escalier is masculine: un escalier. The singular names the staircase; les escaliers is the plural.

anchor.text: Finnish dušši is a useful spoken neighbour of douche. Picture the water running in your hotel shower.

shower.soundFi: Ou is close to Finnish u; ch sounds like sh. The final e is silent.

article.note: Douche is feminine: une douche. Learn the article with the hotel-room object.

anchor.text: Picture the folded towel on the hotel bed: une serviette propre. Add de table later when the same noun means napkin.

towel.soundFi: Ie glides into an e-like vowel. The double tt is not Finnish long tt; the last e is silent.

article.note: Serviette is feminine: une serviette. It keeps the same gender in une serviette de table, a napkin.

anchor.text: Petit means small; petit déjeuner is breakfast in France. Picture the small morning meal before déjeuner, lunch.

breakfast.soundFi: The t of petit is silent before déjeuner. Eu in déjeuner is ö-like, and -er ends in an e-like vowel.

article.note: Petit déjeuner is masculine because déjeuner is the main noun: un petit déjeuner.

anchor.text: Spot jour, day, inside séjour. Picture the stretch of days you spend in Angers: mon séjour dure une semaine.

stay.soundFi: É is e-like; j is voiced sh, not Finnish j. Ou is close to Finnish u and the final r is heard.

article.note: Séjour is masculine: un séjour. The jour part is also masculine in un jour.

anchor.text: Nuit means night; nuitée packages one night of accommodation. Picture a single hotel-calendar square with its price.

overnight-stay.soundFi: Start ui with a Finnish-y-like position and glide quickly into i. Ée ends in one e-like vowel, not two syllables.

article.note: Nuitée is feminine, like nuit, night. Store une nuitée as one billed night of accommodation.

anchor.text: Picture the hotel’s green vacancy indicator and ask une chambre disponible ? The word attaches to the free room.

available.soundFi: The n is pronounced here, not nasal: it starts the next syllable. The final e is usually silent.
